description: We are two students of EPFL, Lausanne passionate about astronomy, coding and robotics.
summary: We developed CALLUNA, an interactive 3D lunar exploration and mission-planning web application built with React, Three.js, and a Python FastAPI scientific backend. Designed to make complex lunar data accessible to mission planners, educators, and the public, CALLUNA allows users to double-click anywhere on a high-resolution 3D Moon—including the challenging polar regions—and select custom mission dates to immediately assess landing feasibility.   To directly address the challenge, our backend integrates authentic NASA LRO/LOLA topography with JPL Horizons ephemerides to compute local slope, terrain-induced shadows, solar illumination windows, and direct-to-Earth radio communication over time. An interactive 2D polar horizon radar visualizes the exact trajectories of the Sun and Earth relative to surrounding crater rims and mountains, while customizable mission thresholds evaluate site viability in real time.   CALLUNA matters because selecting a lunar landing site requires balancing extreme thermal, power, and communication constraints—especially near the lunar South Pole. By turning fragmented scientific datasets into a single-click, intuitive visual decision tool, CALLUNA bridges the gap between raw planetary telemetry and actionable mission design.
details:
What it does and how it works : CALLUNA is an interactive 3D lunar mission planner and landing-site evaluator designed to make planetary exploration data intuitive and actionable. Users explore a high-resolution 3D globe of the Moon, double-click anywhere on the surface (including challenging polar regions like Shackleton Crater) or enter exact coordinates, and select custom launch and return dates. The frontend sends these parameters to a Python backend that cross-references real lunar topography with solar and terrestrial ephemerides over the mission window. It then evaluates landing feasibility across terrain slope, solar illumination availability, maximum continuous darkness (battery survival), and direct-to-Earth radio communication windows, displaying both real-time pass/fail diagnostics and an interactive 2D polar horizon radar.

Benefits and intended impact Existing planetary datasets are often fragmented across complex scientific catalogs and command-line tools, making rapid site comparison difficult. CALLUNA bridges the gap between raw telemetry and human decision-making by combining global 3D spatial context with local sky visibility in a single, zero-setup desktop interface. Its intended impact is twofold: enabling mission engineers to rapidly prototype and stress-test landing scenarios under customizable hardware profiles (e.g., heavy landers, light rovers, or long-duration missions), while providing students, educators, and space enthusiasts with an accessible, visual way to understand the extreme environmental constraints of lunar exploration—especially at the lunar South Pole.

Tools, coding languages, hardware, and software used

  • Frontend: JavaScript (ES6+), React, Vite, Three.js (@react-three/fiber and @react-three/drei), HTML5/SVG, and CSS3 for the 3D WebGL lunar globe, polar tile rendering, and custom HUD.
  • Backend: Python 3, FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy, Pandas, and Requests for astronomical modeling, terrain gradient/horizon-mask computations, and REST API endpoints.
  • Scientific Data Sources: NASA Moon Trek / LRO imagery, LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter) digital elevation models, and NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris services.
  • Deployment & Dev Tools: Git/GitHub, VS Code, and a custom Windows batch launcher (.bat) with automated Python virtual environment provisioning so the entire application runs locally with a single double-click.

Creativity Instead of presenting static tables or abstract elevation charts, CALLUNA pairs a 3D interactive lunar globe with a synchronized 2D Local Sky & Horizon Mask radar. As the user scrubs through the mission timeline, the radar dynamically plots the exact paths of the Sun and Earth against the site’s 360° surrounding mountain and crater-rim profile—visually revealing when nearby relief blocks sunlight or cuts off direct radio contact with Earth.

Key factors our team considered

  • Polar geometry & distortion: Standard equirectangular maps distort heavily near ±90° latitude, so we engineered dedicated polar projection handling and constant-size screen-space crosshairs to ensure millimeter-accurate selection at the South Pole.
  • Real-world engineering trade-offs: We modeled interdependent constraints—such as continuous night duration versus battery autonomy, local terrain slope versus lander stability, and simultaneous Sun-Earth visibility for active surface operations—while allowing users to customize thresholds in real time.
  • Accessibility & portability: To ensure judges, educators, and teammates could run the tool effortlessly without installing Node.js or configuring servers, we bundled the pre-compiled frontend directly into FastAPI with an automated one-click launcher.
